title: Open problem: Does realised cross-arm clinician exposure move cluster-randomised and stepped-wedge trial
statement: Does realised cross-arm clinician exposure move cluster-randomised and stepped-wedge trial effect estimates, and what is the professional-level ICC that design methodology needs and cannot get? Asked twice in medicine's own literature and answered in neither. Magill et al. 2019 counted 82 of 234 trial articles (35%) reporting that staff delivered the active intervention in the control arm, 76 of those 82 citing one clinician delivering both treatments, with a median contamination of 13% (IQR 5–33%) over 23 binary-outcome trials whose unit is CONTROL-ARM PARTICIPANTS, and called for a systematic review of the design. Keogh-Brown et al. 2007 set out nineteen years earlier to quantify the effect of contamination on magnitude and precision, found that “Few relevant studies quantified contamination” and made reporting its extent “a priority”; its all-studies analysis found trials avoiding contamination “tended to have larger effects” while concluding “there is no clear evidence that the effectiveness estimate in trials that do not avoid contamination is biased”, and its high-quality reminder subset runs the other way, so the DIRECTION is genuinely open rather than merely unquantified. Three limbs, in order of cost. (i) The systematic review Magill asks for, executable from the public record: compare within-study cluster-level against participant-level allocation across the trials that ran both, on more than the 4 trials and 21 outcomes (8 of 21 attenuated, one tie, “just under half” in the anticipated direction) that Magill's own null rests on. (ii) The professional-level ICC, which Moerbeek & Safarkhani 2018 ask for in print — for cluster-randomised trials with crossed random effects “such estimates are hardly available in the literature” — and which their own worked example has to assume (ru = .3 from a published power analysis, rv = .1 and rw = .05 “without further justification”); they issue NO call to measure crossing FREQUENCY, so that is not what this row routes from them. (iii) A within-trial refit under a crossed clinician random effect, reporting how far the estimate and interval move against the published analysis, in a trial that holds provider identifiers. What this row does NOT route, because it is asked and partly answered: the article- and protocol-level prevalence of the phenomenon (Magill above; Jacobsen & Wood 2020, 14 of 100 protocols at high contamination risk with 10 of those 14 therapist-related, and only 57 of 100 protocols stating clearly who delivered the intervention, which is the ceiling on any literature-assembled frame). Nor is the causal contrast identified from a single realised cluster-level assignment, which the posing record concedes, so limb (iii) is a model-sensitivity comparison and must be reported as one. Adjacent and not prior art: Xierali 2018 reports 63.2% of 20,116 Georgia Medicaid-registered physicians at multiple sites with a mean of 3.3 — a marginal workforce rate, not a trial cohort, and internally inconsistent with its own Discussion statement that two thirds of Georgia physicians practised in one service location; Wilson-Aggarwal et al., Commun Med 2:165 (2022) supplies the instrument (staff located by ward and day from EHR pseudonymous identifiers plus door-access logs) with no trial and no arms.

inputs.source_showing_it_is_open: Magill et al., BMC Med Res Methodol 19:4 (2019), doi 10.1186/s12874-018-0646-z — “a systematic review of this particular trial design is needed”, verbatim, publisher route, verified at first hand post-batch; Keogh-Brown et al., Health Technol Assess 11(43) (2007), doi 10.3310/hta11430 — “it is a priority to report the extent, nature and effects of contamination” and CACE “if it can be measured”, read at executive-summary plus Chapters 1–2 level post-batch; Moerbeek & Safarkhani, J Educ Behav Stat 43(2):159–181 (2018), doi 10.3102/1076998617730303 — crossed-factor estimates “are hardly available in the literature”, SAGE full-text PDF, two independent fetches agreeing. All three verified post-batch by separate fresh-context readers; see the Verification block of UQ-20261017-37 in unasked-ledger.md for the unit corrections those readers made to the figures above.
inputs.tier: A for limb (i), which is public-record systematic-review work and is what the posing paper actually asks for. C for limbs (ii) and (iii): both need trial-held provider identifiers linked to arm and calendar window, so they are executable only by a trial team or an embedded-trial consortium — the instrument exists (Wilson-Aggarwal 2022) but the data are inside the trials. Limb (i) should come first regardless of access, because a null there changes what limbs (ii) and (iii) are worth.
inputs.how: Work it as PROMPT.md describes. Open the source first and confirm the problem is still open. State exactly what you established and what you did not.
